bibliography.abstract: Reliable lane markings are important for both human drivers and automated driving systems, but their condition is still commonly assessed through manual inspection. Existing autonomous-driving datasets primarily support lane detection and scene understanding and usually lack maintenance-oriented labels for lane-marking visibility, continuity, or degradation. In this study, we present a geo-referenced smartphone dashcam dataset and baseline framework for lane-marking quality assessment. The dataset contains 63,839 road-facing frames collected across South Texas using a GPS-enabled dashcam application. A subset of 3,339 frames is matched with OpenStreetMap-derived lane-count labels, which are used as weak supervision for lane-count regression and map-consistency evaluation. We propose three lane-quality measures: Contrast Stability Index (CSI), which captures lane-background contrast using Laplacian responses; Line Continuity Ratio (LCR), which estimates structural continuity using edge and Hough-line evidence; and Regression Lane Confidence Score (RLCS), which measures agreement between predicted and map-derived lane counts on matched frames. The baseline prediction models attained strong performance, with CSI (MAE $0.039$, $R^2=0.97$) and LCR (MAE $0.093$, $R^2=0.84$). Notably, CSI and LCR are no-reference, segmentation-derived quality metrics that can be computed without dense human labels. In a pilot validation using 50 human-ranked images, these proposed lane-specific metrics show stronger rank agreement with human lane-quality ordering (e.g., Spearman's $ρ=0.7316$ and Kendall's $τ=0.5472$ for LCR) than general image-quality measures such as PSNR, SSIM, BRISQUE, NIQE, and LPIPS. We believe the dataset, metrics, and baseline provide an initial step toward scalable, low-cost, location-aware lane-marking quality assessment. Data and code: https://github.com/Shaif95/Road_Quality
bibliography.title: Deep Learning-Based Road Lane Quality Assessment from Egocentric Dashcam Video

en.caveats: Human validation of the proposed quality metrics relies on a small pilot sample of 50 ranked images within a single geographic region.
en.what: The authors developed a baseline framework and a geo-referenced smartphone dashcam dataset containing 63,839 frames from South Texas to automate lane-marking quality evaluations. The approach introduces three specific quality metrics: Contrast Stability Index ($R^2=0.97$), Line Continuity Ratio ($R^2=0.84$), and Regression Lane Confidence Score based on 3,339 OpenStreetMap-matched frames. In a pilot test of 50 images, these metrics achieved stronger rank correlation with human quality ratings (Spearman's $\rho=0.7316$ for continuity) than standard image-quality algorithms.
en.why: Road infrastructure monitoring can shift from manual field inspections to automated, low-cost video surveys using metrics specifically tailored to lane visibility and map consistency rather than general image metrics.
